Purpose of review

This review critically evaluates evidence on sleep spindles (SP), slow oscillations (SOs), and their coordination in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (AD), focusing on their relationships with cognition, AD biomarkers, and their therapeutic potential.

Recent findings

Longitudinal studies associate greater SP and/or SO activity with better cognition and favourable amyloid and tau profiles after clinical onset. Spindle and SO coupling may index network integrity. Preserved NREM sleep oscillations are associated with lower orexin concentrations and weaker adverse relationships between orexin and cognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes. Closed-loop acoustic stimulation and slow-oscillatory transcranial direct-current stimulation can modify SO activity, spindle activity, and coupling, although cognitive and biomarker benefits remain uncertain. Spindle-SO activity, including their temporal coupling, are associated with cognition and AD biomarkers across the disease continuum. Closed-loop acoustic and electrical stimulation can modify these oscillations, but biomarker-characterized trials in MCI and AD are needed to determine whether treatment produces durable cognitive and biomarker benefits.","affiliation":"Centre de Recherche de L'Institut Universitaire de Gériatrie de Montréal (CRIUGM), Centre Intégré Universitaire de Santé Et Services, Sociaux du Centre-Sud-de-L'île-de-Montréal, Montreal, H3W 1W5, Canada. variable pharmacodynamic sensitivity, and limited physiological reserve. The extent of these differences depends on the underlying condition, disease severity, comorbidity, and treatment setting. These issues are common in older adults, patients with obesity or obstructive sleep apnoea, organ dysfunction, cardiovascular vulnerability, critical illness, and neurological or psychiatric comorbidity. Conventional sedatives may be poorly tolerated in these settings. Propofol can cause hypotension and respiratory depression. Midazolam may lead to delayed recovery and accumulation. Dexmedetomidine may be limited by bradycardia and slow onset. Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine that undergoes rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis and can be antagonised with flumazenil. This narrative review examines its pharmacology, clinical evidence, and practical use across nine vulnerable populations. The synthesis prioritised population-specific clinical studies, pharmacokinetic studies, comparative trials, systematic reviews, and major guidelines. For short procedures, the most consistent evidence concerns older adults and haemodynamically vulnerable patients, in whom remimazolam has often been associated with less hypotension than propofol and faster recovery than midazolam. These findings are based mainly on short-term physiological and recovery outcomes. Evidence in mild to moderate hepatic or renal dysfunction is supportive but remains sparse in severe disease. Data for obesity or obstructive sleep apnoea, prolonged ICU sedation, paediatric care, obstetrics, and neurological or psychiatric vulnerability are limited or indirect. Remimazolam should therefore be considered according to the clinical objective, the expected duration and depth of sedation, opioid exposure, airway risk, and organ reserve. Its pharmacological advantages have not yet been shown to improve delirium, cognition, mechanical ventilation, functional recovery, or long-term safety. Further studies should focus on population-specific dosing models and patient-centred outcomes.","affiliation":"Department of Anesthesiology, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical
